rules.text: Use a Parshall flume when flow must be measured in an open channel with little head loss.
rules.because: Head loss is much smaller than for a weir (the Arkon guide puts it at three to four times smaller), and accuracy of 2 to 5 percent is reported under normal conditions.

rules.text: The flume keeps solids moving, so it does not silt up the way a weir pool can.
rules.because: Velocity through the flume is high enough to prevent suspended solids settling.

rules.text: A flume tolerates a high downstream water level before its calibration stops applying.
rules.because: Free flow holds up to a transition submergence of 56 to 78 percent depending on size, so downstream conditions can vary widely.

source.loc: Table 2; Definition of free and submerged flow

rules.text: Do not choose a flume where the channel has very little fall unless submerged operation is designed for.
rules.because: With a very flat grade the crest cannot be set high enough for free flow, and then both Ha and Hb must be measured.

rules.text: The flow is submerged: the free-flow table no longer applies. Read both Ha and Hb and use the submerged-flow calibration.
rules.because: Submergence Hb/Ha is above the transition value for this flume size.

rules.text: Submergence is above 0.7, the upper limit named in the Arkon guide; the discharge equation has to be adjusted.
rules.because: The guide lists the maximum submergence ratio per size (0.6 for P1-P5, 0.7 for P6-P9).

rules.text: The flume is too close to a bend or drop. Move it so the approach flow is smooth and evenly distributed.
rules.because: Arkon asks for at least 12 W from the end of a curve (and at least 30 W after a drop wall, depending on depth and floor shape).

rules.text: The flume sits too near a gate. Gate operation causes unbalanced flow and surging at the flume.
rules.because: The Utah report says not to place a flume too near a gate.

rules.text: Debris is larger than the throat can pass. Add a screen upstream.
rules.because: The Arkon guide limits freely passing debris to 0.8 times the throat width W.

rules.text: Throat width is outside the usual one-third to one-half of the channel width. Recheck the size selection.
rules.because: The Utah report says the throat is normally one-third to one-half of the channel width.

rules.text: Water temperature is above the 80 degC maximum stated for the polypropylene flume.
rules.because: Operating limit in the Arkon guide; the water must also never be allowed to freeze.

rules.text: Build to the table dimensions, especially the entrance and throat. The converging floor must be level in both directions, and the crest straight and level.
rules.because: The calibration only holds for the standard geometry and a level approach floor.

rules.text: If the built throat width differs from the specified width, scale the table discharge by built width divided by specified width.
rules.because: Worked example: a 2 ft flume built at 2.10 ft gives a factor of 1.05.

rules.text: Check the entrance floor level a few months after start-up and again each year. Remove moss and debris and clean encrustation.
rules.because: Flumes settle, and a tilted or settled flume reads wrong; settlement at the exit is the most common case.

rules.text: Clean the flume surface, float shaft and connecting pipe once a year, and clean an ultrasonic probe within six months.
rules.because: Incrustation and impurities degrade the reading.
